On the log-concavity of the Wright function

Rui A. C. Ferreira Address: Grupo Física-Matemática, Faculdade de Ciências, Universidade de Lisboa, Av. Prof. Gama Pinto, 2, 1649-003, Lisboa. Email: raferreira@fc.ul.pt and Thomas Simon Address: Laboratoire Paul Painlevé, Université de Lille, 59000 Lille. Email: thomas.simon@univ-lille.fr
Abstract.

We investigate the log-concavity on the half-line of the Wright function ϕ⁡(−α,β,−x),\phi(-\alpha,\beta,-x), in the probabilistic setting α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and β≥0.\beta\geq 0. Applications are given to the construction of generalized entropies associated to the corresponding Mittag-Leffler function. A natural conjecture for the equivalence between the log-concavity of the Wright function and the existence of such generalized entropies is formulated. The problem is solved for β≥α\beta\geq\alpha and in the classical case β=1−α\beta=1-\alpha of the Mittag-Leffler distribution, which exhibits a certain critical parameter α∗=0.771667​…\alpha_{*}=0.771667... defined implicitly on the Gamma function and characterizing the log-concavity. We also prove that the probabilistic Wright functions are always unimodal, and that they are multiplicatively strongly unimodal if and only if β≥α\beta\geq\alpha or α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2 and β=0.\beta=0.

Key words and phrases: 
Bell-shape; Beta distribution; Entropy; Log-concavity; Meijer GG-function; Mittag-Leffler distribution; Mittag-Leffler function; Unimodality; Wright function
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
26A33; 26A51; 33C60; 33E12; 60E15; 62E15; 94A17

1. Introduction

The Wright function is defined as the entire function

ϕ⁡(ρ,β,z)=∑n≥0znn!​Γ​(β+ρ​n),β,z∈ℂ,ρ>−1.\phi(\rho,\beta,z)\;=\;\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}}{n!\,\Gamma(\beta+\rho n)},\qquad\beta,z\in{\mathbb{C}},\;\rho>-1.

In the case ρ=0,\rho=0, it is an exponential function and in the other cases it is an entire function of order 1/(1+ρ).1/(1+\rho). In the early literature, the Wright function is sometimes called the generalized Bessel function because of the following representation in the case ρ=1\rho=1:

Jν(z)=(z/2)νϕ(1,ν+1,−z2/4).J_{\nu}(z)\;=\;(z/2)^{\nu}\phi(1,\nu+1,-z^{2}/4).

The Wright function admits an integral representation given by

ϕ⁡(ρ,β,z)=12​π​i​∫Ht−β​et+z​t−ρ​𝑑t,\phi(\rho,\beta,z)\;=\;\frac{1}{2\pi{\rm i}}\int_{H}t^{-\beta}\,e^{t+zt^{-\rho}}\,dt, (1)

where HH is the classical Hankel contour between e−i​π​∞e^{-{\rm i}\pi}\infty and ei​π​∞e^{{\rm i}\pi}\infty encircling the origin counterclockwise. The Wright function was introduced in [39, 40] for ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 in connection with the asymptotic study of partitions, and later studied in [41] for all ρ>−1.\rho>-1. In the recent literature, the function ϕ⁡(ρ,β,z)\phi(\rho,\beta,z) with ρ∈(−1,0)\rho\in(-1,0) is sometimes called the Wright function of the second kind - see [7] and the references therein. There is a well-known relationship between the Wright function and the two-parameter Mittag-Leffler function

Eα,β​(z)=∑n≥0znΓ⁡(β+α​n),β,z∈ℂ,α>0,E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)\;=\;\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}}{\Gamma(\beta+\alpha n)},\qquad\beta,z\in{\mathbb{C}},\;\alpha>0,

which is illustrated by the Laplace transforms

∫0∞ϕ(ρ,β,x)e−x​tdx=Eρ,β(1/t),β∈ℂ,ρ,t>0\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(\rho,\beta,x)\,e^{-xt}\,dx\;=\;E_{\rho,\beta}(1/t),\qquad\beta\in{\mathbb{C}},\;\rho,t>0

obtained by direct summation, and

∫0∞ϕ⁡(ρ,β,−x)​e−x​t​𝑑x=E−ρ,β−ρ​(−t),β∈ℂ,ρ∈(−1,0),t>0\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(\rho,\beta,-x)\,e^{-xt}\,dx\;=\;E_{-\rho,\beta-\rho}(-t),\qquad\beta\in{\mathbb{C}},\;\rho\in(-1,0),\;t>0 (2)

obtained from Fubini’s theorem applied to (1) and the usual contour representation of Eα,β​(z).E_{\alpha,\beta}(z). We refer to Chapter 18 in [11] and Section 2.3. in [17] for more material on this classical relationship.

The connection between Wright functions and probability theory is relevant for ρ∈(−1,0].\rho\in(-1,0]. In this case indeed, it follows on the one hand from the exponential asymptotic expansion in [41] that ϕ⁡(ρ,β,z)\phi(\rho,\beta,z) is integrable on ℝ−{\mathbb{R}}^{-} and on the other hand, from (2) and the complete monotonicity of Mittag-Leffler functions on ℝ−{\mathbb{R}}^{-} originally characterized in [35], that it is positive on ℝ−{\mathbb{R}}^{-} if β≥0\beta\geq 0 and ρ∈(−1,0].\rho\in(-1,0]. This shows that the function

x↦φα,β​(x)=Γ⁡(α+β)​ϕ​(−α,β,−x)x\mapsto\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\;=\;\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)\,\phi(-\alpha,\beta,-x) (3)

is the density of a positive random variable 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} for all α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) and β≥0.\beta\geq 0. Expanding the Laplace transform (2) implies that this random variable has Mellin transform

𝔼⁡[𝐌α,βs]=(1)s(α+β)α​s,s>−1,{\mathbb{E}}[{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}^{s}]\;=\;\frac{(1)_{s}}{(\alpha+\beta)_{\alpha s}},\qquad s>-1, (4)

with the usual Pochhammer notation (a)s=Γ⁡(a+s)/Γ⁡(a)(a)_{s}={\Gamma}(a+s)/{\Gamma}(a) for a>0a>0. With the terminology of [22], this shows that 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} has moments of Gamma type. Observe that (4) can be extended to α=1,β>0\alpha=1,\beta>0 with 𝐌1,β=𝐁1,β{\bf M}_{1,\beta}={\bf B}_{1,\beta} where, here and throughout, 𝐁a,b{\bf B}_{a,b} denotes the beta random variable with density

Γ⁡(a+b)Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)​xa−1​(1−x)b−1​𝟏(0,1)​(x).\frac{{\Gamma}(a+b)}{{\Gamma}(a){\Gamma}(b)}\,x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}{\bf 1}_{(0,1)}(x).

Notice that the right-hand side of (4) is never the Mellin transform of a non-negative function for α<0\alpha<0 or {α>0,β<0}\{\alpha>0,\beta<0\} since it then vanishes inside the definition strip, or for α>1\alpha>1 since the support of the function would then be {0}.\{0\}. In the following, we will call the set {α∈[0,1],β≥0}\{\alpha\in[0,1],\;\beta\geq 0\} the admissible set for 𝐌α,β.{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}. Except in the degenerate case {α=1,β=0}\{\alpha=1,\beta=0\} with 𝐌1,0=1,{\bf M}_{1,0}=1, the random variable 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} has always a smooth density over its support which is given by φα,β​(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x) for α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) and by β​(1−x)β−1​𝟏(0,1)​(x)=φ1,β​(x)\beta(1-x)^{\beta-1}{\bf 1}_{(0,1)}(x)=\varphi_{1,\beta}(x) for α=1.\alpha=1. It is easy to see from (4) that Supp 𝐌α,β=ℝ+{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}\,=\,{\mathbb{R}}^{+} for all α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) and β≥0.\beta\geq 0. Observe also that 𝐌0,β=𝐋,{\bf M}_{0,\beta}={\bf L}, the standard exponential random variable, for all β≥0.\beta\geq 0. When α∈(0,1),\alpha\in(0,1), the densities φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} are mostly non-explicit. One purpose of this paper is to show some basic, albeit non-trivial, properties of these densities, which transfer immediately to the Wright functions of the second kind. Our first finding is the following.

Theorem A​​ .

The random variable 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} is unimodal.

This result is easy to prove for β≥α\beta\geq\alpha and the density φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} is then non-increasing. For β<α,\beta<\alpha, the density is increasing-then-decreasing and the proof, which relies on strong unimodality and a detailed analysis of the distributions with binomial moments introduced in [30], is more involved. In the case β=1−α,\beta=1-\alpha, the random variable 𝐌α,1−α=𝐌α{\bf M}_{\alpha,1-\alpha}={\bf M}_{\alpha} has a so-called Mittag-Leffler distribution with moment generating function

𝔼⁡[ez​𝐌α]=Eα​(z),{\mathbb{E}}[e^{z{\bf M}_{\alpha}}]\;=\;E_{\alpha}(z), (5)

where Eα​(z)=Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha}(z)=E_{\alpha,1}(z) stands for the classical Mittag-Leffler function, which we extend to E0​(z)=1/(1−z)E_{0}(z)=1/(1-z) on {ℜ(z)<1}\{\Re(z)<1\} for α=0\alpha=0. If 1−α≤α,1-\alpha\leq\alpha, the unimodality of 𝐌α{\bf M}_{\alpha} follows then from the well-known fact - see Section 8 in [6] and the references therein - that it is distributed as the positive part of a real spectrally negative stable random variable with parameter 1/α∈[1,2],1/\alpha\in[1,2], which is unimodal by Yamazato’s theorem - see Theorem 53.1 in [33].

The random variable 𝐌α{\bf M}_{\alpha} plays a central role in various probabilistic contexts. If {Zt(α),t≥0}\{Z^{(\alpha)}_{t},\;t\geq 0\} denotes the α−\alpha-stable subordinator with Laplace transform 𝔼⁡[e−λ​Zt(α)]=e−t​λα{\mathbb{E}}[e^{-\lambda Z^{(\alpha)}_{t}}]=e^{-t\lambda^{\alpha}} for t,λ≥0t,\lambda\geq 0 and if we set 𝐙α=Z1(α),{\bf Z}_{\alpha}=Z^{(\alpha)}_{1}, then it is classical and easy to show by moment identification and self-similarity that

𝐌α=d𝐙α−α=dinf{t>0,Zt(α)>1}.{\bf M}_{\alpha}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf Z}_{\alpha}^{-\alpha}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\inf\{t>0,\;Z^{(\alpha)}_{t}>1\}.

The Mittag-Leffler random variable also appears in limit theorems for occupation times of Markov processes [5], Pólya urn schemes [21], coalescents [31], and elephant random walks [3]. This list is non-exhaustive and we refer to the survey paper [19] for an account on 𝐌α{\bf M}_{\alpha} and other related random variables. It is natural to ask for basic distributional properties of 𝐌α,{\bf M}_{\alpha}, and we focus in this paper on the log-concavity of the density. This property is equivalent to the strong additive unimodality of 𝐌α{\bf M}_{\alpha} in the non-degenerate case α≠1\alpha\neq 1 by Ibragimov’s theorem [20], and can hence be viewed as a refinement of unimodality. We prove the following rather unexpected characterization.

Theorem B​​ .

The density of 𝐌α{\bf M}_{\alpha} is log-concave if and only if α≤α∗,\alpha\leq\alpha_{*}, where α∗=0.771667​…\alpha_{*}=0.771667... is the unique solution on (0,1)(0,1) of the equation

1Γ​(1−2​α)2=1Γ⁡(1−α)​Γ​(1−3​α)⋅\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(1-2\alpha)^{2}}\;=\;\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(1-\alpha)\,{\Gamma}(1-3\alpha)}\cdot

Some graphical evidence for the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the above equation defining the critical parameter α∗\alpha_{*} is given in Figure 1 below, where the property is also checked rigorously. For α∈(1/2,1),\alpha\in(1/2,1), the above result has immediate applications to the integro-differential equation

u⁡(t,x)=f⁡(x)+1Γ⁡(2​α)​∫0t(t−s)2​α−1​Δ​u​(s,x)​𝑑s,t>0,x∈ℝ,u(t,x)\;=\;f(x)\;+\;\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(2\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}\,(t-s)^{2\alpha-1}\Delta u(s,x)\,ds,\qquad t>0,\,x\in{\mathbb{R}},

which was studied in [14] as an interpolation between the heat equation (α=1/2\alpha=1/2) and the wave equation (α=1\alpha=1), and whose unique solution is expressed in Formula (1) of [15] as

uα​(t,x)=12​(𝔼⁡[f⁡(x+tα​𝐌α)+f⁡(x−tα​𝐌α)]).u_{\alpha}(t,x)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathbb{E}}\left[f(x+t^{\alpha}{\bf M}_{\alpha})\,+\,f(x-t^{\alpha}{\bf M}_{\alpha})\right]\right).

If the initial data f⁡(x)f(x) is unimodal on ℝ,{\mathbb{R}}, as it often happens for natural phenomena governed by heat or waves, then Theorem B and Ibragimov’s theorem imply that for every t>0,t>0, the solution uα​(t,x)u_{\alpha}(t,x) will be the superposition of two unimodal functions for α≤α∗,\alpha\leq\alpha_{*}, and of two functions which may have multiple modes if α>α∗.\alpha>\alpha_{*}. In other words, the spatial behaviour of the solution uα​(t,x)u_{\alpha}(t,x) is similar to the classical solution

u1​(t,x)=12​(𝔼⁡[f⁡(x+t)+f⁡(x−t)])u_{1}(t,x)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathbb{E}}\left[f(x+t)\,+\,f(x-t)\right]\right)

of the wave equation for α∈(1/2,α∗],\alpha\in(1/2,\alpha_{*}], and possibly different for α∈(α∗,1).\alpha\in(\alpha_{*},1). We refer to [7, 17] and the references therein for more general integro-differential equations and related physical problems, also involving the random variables 𝐌α,0,𝐌α,α{\bf M}_{\alpha,0},{\bf M}_{\alpha,\alpha} and 𝐌α,1.{\bf M}_{\alpha,1}.

Our original motivation for Theorem B stems from the so-called generalized entropies on a finite state space. If p={pi,i=1,…,n}p=\{p_{i},\;i=1,\ldots,n\} is a probability on a finite set, then its generalized entropy is defined as

S⁡(p)=∑i=1ng⁡(pi)S(p)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}g(p_{i}) (6)

where gg is some function from [0,1][0,1] to ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} which satisfies the three Shannon-Khinchin principles. The latter are simply given by: (i) g⁡(0)=g⁡(1)=0g(0)=g(1)=0; (ii) gg is continuous; (iii) gg is concave, and we refer to [1, 12] and the references therein for more on this topic. The classical entropy corresponds to the function g⁡(x)=−x​log⁡x,g(x)=-x\log x, which involves the natural logarithm. Because of its very simple series representation and its absolute monotonicity on the real line, it is sometimes said - see e.g. Chapters 1 and 2 in [18] - that the classical Mittag-Leffler function Eα​(x)E_{\alpha}(x) is for α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] a generalization of the exponential function; we can hence consider its inverse function Eα−1​(x)=logα⁡(x)E_{\alpha}^{-1}(x)=\log_{\alpha}(x) from (0,∞)(0,\infty) to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} as a generalized logarithm. For α<1\alpha<1 however, the polynomial behaviour of EαE_{\alpha} at −∞-\infty makes the continuous extension of −x​logα​(x)-x\log_{\alpha}(x) at zero different from the case α=1.\alpha=1. It is easy to see from the first term in the expansion 18.1.(20) in [11] and from the evaluation Eα​(0)=1E_{\alpha}(0)=1 that the function

gα​(x)=−x​logα⁡(x)+x−1Γ⁡(1−α)g_{\alpha}(x)\;=\;-x\log_{\alpha}(x)\;+\;\frac{x-1}{{\Gamma}(1-\alpha)}

is well defined on [0,1][0,1] with gα​(0)=gα​(1)=0.g_{\alpha}(0)=g_{\alpha}(1)=0. The continuity of gαg_{\alpha} on [0,1][0,1] is plain, and in order to ensure that the functional in (6) with g=gαg=g_{\alpha} defines a generalized entropy we need to study the concavity of gα,g_{\alpha}, which amounts to that of its affine translation x↦−x​logα​x.x\mapsto-x\log_{\alpha}x.

Theorem C​​ .

The function x↦−x​logα​(x)x\mapsto-x\log_{\alpha}(x) is concave on [0,1][0,1] if and only if α≤α∗\alpha\leq\alpha_{*} or α=1.\alpha=1.

The reason why the same critical parameter α∗\alpha_{*} appears in both Theorem B and C is partly explained by the aforementioned connection between the Wright function ϕ⁡(−α,1−α,−x)\phi(-\alpha,1-\alpha,-x) and the classical Mittag-Leffler function EαE_{\alpha}. The if part of Theorem C is indeed a natural consequence of the if part of Theorem B, which is the difficult part of the characterization relying on a certain Meijer G−G-function approximation if α≤1/2,\alpha\leq 1/2, and on a combination of the so-called Yamazato property and the bell-shape property for real stable densities if α>1/2.\alpha>1/2. We refer to Sections 52 and 53 in [33] resp. [27, 28] for extended discussions on the Yamazato property resp. the bell-shape property. The fact that the only if parts are the same in both theorems is however more surprising and we comment on this in Remark 3 below, where we also discuss in the half-Gaussian case α=1/2\alpha=1/2 the equivalence between Theorem C and the classical Sampford inequality on Mill’s ratio.

In view of the previous theorems, it is natural to investigate the log-concavity of the density of 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} for all admissible (α,β).(\alpha,\beta). We can show the following partial result.

Theorem D​​ .

(a) The density of 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} is not log-concave for all β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) and α>α∗​(β),\alpha>\alpha_{*}(\beta), where α∗​(β)\alpha_{*}(\beta) is the unique solution on (0,1)(0,1) of the equation

1Γ​(β−α)2=1Γ⁡(β)​Γ​(β−2​α)⋅\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(\beta-\alpha)^{2}}\;=\;\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(\beta)\,{\Gamma}(\beta-2\alpha)}\cdot

(b) The density of 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} is log-concave in the following situations.

(i) For all α∈[0,4/5]\alpha\in[0,4/5] and β=0.\beta=0.

(ii) For all α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] and β≥α.\beta\geq\alpha.

The necessary condition in Part (a) and the sufficient condition in Part (b) (i), in the non-trivial situation α∈(α∗,4/5],\alpha\in(\alpha_{*},4/5], are obtained similarly as in Theorem B. However, the sufficient condition given in Part (b) (ii) is more difficult to prove in the relevant case α>4/5.\alpha>4/5. The argument relies on the fractional differential rules connecting Wright functions with one another and on a visual bell-shape property strengthening Theorem A, in addition to all tools already appearing in the proofs of Theorem A and B. Unfortunately, it does not seem to us that these tools are enough to tackle the remaining situations {0<β<α}\{0<\beta<\alpha\} and {α>4/5,β=0},\{\alpha>4/5,\beta=0\}, where we believe that the log-concavity should be characterized by the domain in (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) appearing in the necessity Part (a). We also conjecture, as in Theorem C, that this property is equivalent to the existence of a generalized entropy associated to the Mittag-Leffler function Eα,α+βE_{\alpha,\alpha+\beta} on the negative half-line. More detail on this open problem is given in the last section of the paper. In this last section we also provide some further results related to the above four theorems, on the multiplicative strong unimodality of 𝐌α,β,{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}, on the number of positive zeroes of certain Wright functions, and on the reciprocal convexity of Mittag-Leffler functions on the positive half-line.

2. Proof of Theorem A

The cases α=0,1\alpha=0,1 are immediate and we need to consider the situation α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) only. We begin with the easy case β≥α,\beta\geq\alpha, where we show that φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} is non-increasing and hence unimodal. We use the fractional integration relationship

ϕ⁡(−α,β,−x)=1Γ⁡(γ)​∫x∞ϕ⁡(−α,β−α​γ,−t)​(t−x)γ−1​𝑑t\phi(-\alpha,\beta,-x)\;=\;\frac{1}{\Gamma(\gamma)}\int_{x}^{\infty}\phi(-\alpha,\beta-\alpha\gamma,-t)\,(t-x)^{\gamma-1}\,dt (7)

which is valid for all γ>0\gamma>0 and a straightforward consequence of Fubini’s theorem applied to (1). Choosing γ=1\gamma=1 and differentiating leads to

φα,β′​(x)=−Γ⁡(α+β)​ϕ​(−α,β−α,−x)< 0\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)\;=\;-\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)\,\phi(-\alpha,\beta-\alpha,-x)\;<\;0 (8)

on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} for β≥α,\beta\geq\alpha, which completes the argument. We next consider the case β<α.\beta<\alpha. Observe that here, one has

φα,β′​(0)=(α−β)​Γ​(α+β)Γ⁡(β)​Γ​(β+1−α)> 0\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(0)\;=\;\frac{(\alpha-\beta)\,\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{{\Gamma}(\beta){\Gamma}(\beta+1-\alpha)}\;>\;0

so that φα,β​(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x) is not non-increasing on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} and we need to show that it increases and then decreases. To prove such a property is usually more difficult than the sole monotonicity and we will need less elementary tools. In the case α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2 we use the independent factorization

𝐌α,β=d𝐌α,0×𝐁α,βα,{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf M}_{\alpha,0}\,\times\,{\bf B}_{\alpha,\beta}^{\alpha},

which is valid for all admissible parameters as a direct consequence of (4) and a fractional moment identification. The density of 𝐁α,βα{\bf B}_{\alpha,\beta}^{\alpha} reads

Γ⁡(α+β)Γ⁡(α+1)​Γ​(β)​(1−x1/α)β−1​𝟏(0,1)​(x)\frac{{\Gamma}(\alpha+\beta)}{{\Gamma}(\alpha+1){\Gamma}(\beta)}\,(1-x^{1/\alpha})^{\beta-1}{\bf 1}_{(0,1)}(x)

and is increasing hence unimodal. Besides, setting fαf_{\alpha} for the density of the positive α−\alpha-stable random variable 𝐙α,{\bf Z}_{\alpha}, one has φα,0(x)=αxφα,1−α(x)=x−1/αfα(x−1/α)\varphi_{\alpha,0}(x)=\alpha x\varphi_{\alpha,1-\alpha}(x)=x^{-1/\alpha}f_{\alpha}(x^{-1/\alpha}) with fα​(ex)f_{\alpha}(e^{x}) log-concave on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} for α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2 by the main result of [36]. Hence, the function φα,0​(ex)\varphi_{\alpha,0}(e^{x}) is log-concave on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} for α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2 as well. By the Cuculescu-Theodorescu theorem [9], this implies that 𝐌α,0{\bf M}_{\alpha,0} is multiplicatively strongly unimodal, in other words the independent product of 𝐌α,0{\bf M}_{\alpha,0} with any unimodal random variable remains unimodal. This completes the argument for α≤1/2.\alpha\leq 1/2.

In order to handle the final case α∈(1/2,1)\alpha\in(1/2,1) and β∈[0,α)\beta\in[0,\alpha) we will need the following lemma, which has an independent interest. Recall that a non-negative function on a given interval is absolutely monotone (AM) if it is smooth and all its derivatives are non-negative.

Lemma 1.

For every α∈[1/2,1)\alpha\in[1/2,1) and β∈[0,α),\beta\in[0,\alpha), there exists a random variable 𝐗α,β{\bf X}_{\alpha,\beta} such that

𝔼⁡[𝐗α,βs]=(1)s(α+β)α​s​(2−α−β)(1−α)​s{\mathbb{E}}[{\bf X}_{\alpha,\beta}^{s}]\;=\;\frac{(1)_{s}}{(\alpha+\beta)_{\alpha s}\,(2-\alpha-\beta)_{(1-\alpha)s}}

for all s>−1.s>-1. This random variable has a compact support and an AM density.

This lemma concludes the proof by the same multiplicative strong unimodality argument as above, since (4) gives the independent factorization

𝐌α,β=d𝚪2−α−β1−α×𝐗α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf\Gamma}_{2-\alpha-\beta}^{1-\alpha}\,\times\,{\bf X}_{\alpha,\beta} (9)

where 𝐗α,β{\bf X}_{\alpha,\beta} has an absolutely monotone density and is hence unimodal, whereas 𝚪2−α−β1−α{\bf\Gamma}_{2-\alpha-\beta}^{1-\alpha} is easily seen to be multiplicatively strongy unimodal by the above criterion.

□\square

Proof of Lemma 1. We begin with the case α=1/2.\alpha=1/2. First, the Legendre-Gauss multiplication formula for the Gamma function and a fractional moment identification show that the random variable 𝐗1/2,β{\bf X}_{1/2,\beta} does exist and is distributed, with the notation 𝐁a,0=1{\bf B}_{a,0}=1 for all a>0,a>0, as the independent product

𝐗1/2,β=d 2​𝐁1/2,β×𝐁1,1/2−β,{\bf X}_{1/2,\beta}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;2\,\sqrt{{\bf B}_{1/2,\beta}\,\times\,{\bf B}_{1,1/2-\beta}},

6. Further remarks

6.1. Multiplicative strong unimodality

The proof of Theorem A depends on the notion of multiplicative strong unimodality (MSU), introduced in [9]. For a positive random variable XX with density ff, it is easy to check that the MSU property is implied by the non-increasing character of ff, in other words by the unimodality at zero. When ff is not non-increasing, the MSU property is equivalent by the main result of [9] to the log-concavity of t↦f⁡(et)t\mapsto f(e^{t}) and this property, which we may call MSU*, is invariant under power transformations of XX. Observe that a positive random variable with non-increasing density needs not be MSU*. We refer to [9] and the introduction of [36] for more material on multiplicative strong unimodality. The following characterization, which is a simple consequence of Theorem D, improves on the main result of [36].

Proposition 1.

For every (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) admissible, one has

𝐌α,β​is MSU⟺𝐌α,β​is MSU*⟺β≥α​or​{β=0,α≤1/2}.{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}\,\mbox{is {MSU}}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}\,\mbox{is {MSU*}}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\beta\geq\alpha\,\;\mbox{or}\,\;\{\beta=0,\alpha\leq 1/2\}.
Proof.

Suppose first 0<β<α.0<\beta<\alpha. Then we have φα,β′​(0)>0\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(0)>0 and φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} is not non-increasing on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} so that MSU and MSU* are equivalent properties, tantamount to the non-increasing character of

x↦x​φα,β′​(x)φα,β​(x)⋅x\;\mapsto\;\frac{x\,\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)}{\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)}\cdot

Differentiating, the properties are equivalent to x​φα,β​(x)​φα,β′′​(x)+φα,β​(x)​φα,β′​(x)≤x​φα,β′​(x)2,x\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime\prime}(x)+\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)\,\leq\,x\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)^{2}, which is not true in the neighbourhood of zero since φα,β​(0)​φα,β′​(0)>0.\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(0)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(0)>0. Supposing next β≥α,\beta\geq\alpha, we have seen that φα,β′≤0\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}\leq 0 on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} so that 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} is MSU. Moreover, it is also MSU* since

x​φα,β​(x)​φα,β′′​(x)+φα,β​(x)​φα,β′​(x)≤x​φα,β​(x)​φα,β′′​(x)≤x​φα,β′​(x)2,x\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime\prime}(x)\,+\,\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)\;\leq\;x\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime\prime}(x)\;\leq\;x\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)^{2},

where in the second inequality we have used Theorem D (b) (ii). Finally, if β=0,\beta=0, then φα,0​(0)=0\varphi_{\alpha,0}(0)=0 and MSU and MSU* are again equivalent properties. But since

φα,0​(et)=Γ⁡(1+α)​et​φα,1−α​(et),\varphi_{\alpha,0}(e^{t})\;=\;{\Gamma}(1+\alpha)\,e^{t}\,\varphi_{\alpha,1-\alpha}(e^{t}),

the MSU* property of 𝐌α,0{\bf M}_{\alpha,0} amounts to that of 𝐌α,{\bf M}_{\alpha}, and we can apply the main result of [36].

□\square

Remark 5.

Another direct consequence of Theorem D (b) (ii) and the differential rule (7) is the following Turán inequality for the Wright function, which holds true for all α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and β,x≥0:\beta,x\geq 0:

ϕ⁡(−α,β+α,−x)​ϕ​(−α,β−α,−x)≤ϕ​(−α,β,−x)2.\phi(-\alpha,\beta+\alpha,-x)\,\phi(-\alpha,\beta-\alpha,-x)\;\leq\;\phi(-\alpha,\beta,-x)^{2}.

Observe that the latter inequality is equivalent to the log-concavity of the sequence

{ϕ⁡(−α,β+(n−1)​α,−x),n≥0}\{\phi(-\alpha,\beta+(n-1)\alpha,-x),\;n\geq 0\}

for all α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and β,x≥0.\beta,x\geq 0. There is a vast recent literature on Turán inequalities for special functions and we refer to [8] for a survey. See also [24] and the references therein for results and conjectures in the framework of Meijer G−G-functions. Notice that in many papers on Turán inequalities, the coefficients in the involved series have constant sign, which is not the case in our framework by the negativities of −α-\alpha and −x-x.

6.2. On the number of positive zeroes of the Wright function

In this paragraph, we briefly comment on how some of our findings can be applied to investigate the exact number of positive zeroes of Wright functions, in a non-probabilistic setting. Our results are only partial as a simple consequence of Theorem A and Lemma 2, and this topic certainly deserves a deeper study. For any ρ>0,\rho>0, the Wright function ϕ⁡(ρ,β,z)\phi(\rho,\beta,z) has an infinite number of zeroes given by the Hadamard factorization, and it was shown in Theorem 1 of [2] that the zeroes are all negative for β>0\beta>0 and that there are [β]+1[\beta]+1 non-negative zeroes for β<0\beta<0 and ρ∈(0,1].\rho\in(0,1]. The situation is however more complicated for ρ∈(−1,0),\rho\in(-1,0), since then the Wright function has order greater than one - see [41]. Setting 𝒩ρ,β,+=♯⁡{x>0,ϕ⁡(ρ,β,−x)= 0},{\mathcal{N}}_{\rho,\beta,+}=\sharp\{x>0,\;\phi(\rho,\beta,-x)\,=\,0\}, we see by the discussion made in the introduction that

𝒩ρ,β,+= 0⟺β≥ 0{\mathcal{N}}_{\rho,\beta,+}\;=\;0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta\,\geq\,0

for every ρ∈(−1,0).\rho\in(-1,0). In the non-probabilistic setting, we can show the following.

Proposition 2.

For every ρ∈(−1,−1/2]\rho\in(-1,-1/2], one has

𝒩ρ,β,+= 1for β∈[−1,0)and𝒩ρ,β,+= 2for β∈[2ρ,−1).{\mathcal{N}}_{\rho,\beta,+}\;=\;1\quad\mbox{for $\beta\in[-1,0)$}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad{\mathcal{N}}_{\rho,\beta,+}\;=\;2\quad\mbox{for $\beta\in[2\rho,-1).$}
Proof.

If ρ∈(−1,0)\rho\in(-1,0) and β∈[ρ,0),\beta\in[\rho,0), we know from (7) that

ϕ⁡(ρ,β,−x)=−ϕ′​(ρ,β−ρ,−x)\phi(\rho,\beta,-x)\;=\;-\phi^{\prime}(\rho,\beta-\rho,-x)

and the function on the right-hand side is negative-then-positive on (0,∞)(0,\infty) by Theorem A, with an isolated zero on (0,∞)(0,\infty) by the real analyticity of Wright functions. If ρ∈(−1,−1/2]\rho\in(-1,-1/2] and β∈(−1,ρ),\beta\in(-1,\rho), we know from (7) that

ϕ⁡(ρ,β,−x)=ϕ′′​(ρ,β−2​ρ,−x)\phi(\rho,\beta,-x)\;=\;\phi^{\prime\prime}(\rho,\beta-2\rho,-x) (17)

and the function on the right-hand side is also negative-then-positive on (0,∞),(0,\infty), by Lemma 2 and the fact that ϕ⁡(ρ,β,0)=1/Γ⁡(β)<0,\phi(\rho,\beta,0)=1/{\Gamma}(\beta)<0, with again an isolated zero on (0,∞).(0,\infty). If ρ∈(−1,−1/2]\rho\in(-1,-1/2] and β=−1,\beta=-1, then ϕ⁡(ρ,−1,0)=0\phi(\rho,-1,0)=0 and ϕ⁡(ρ,−1,−x)<0\phi(\rho,-1,-x)<0 in a neighbourhood of zero, so that again 𝒩ρ,−1,+=1.{\mathcal{N}}_{\rho,-1,+}=1. Finally, if ρ∈(−1,−1/2)\rho\in(-1,-1/2) and β∈[2ρ,−1),\beta\in[2\rho,-1), then (17) and Lemma 2 with ϕ⁡(ρ,β,0)=1/Γ⁡(β)>0\phi(\rho,\beta,0)=1/{\Gamma}(\beta)>0 show that ϕ⁡(ρ,β,−x)\phi(\rho,\beta,-x) is positive-then-negative-then-positive on (0,∞),(0,\infty), with two isolated zeroes.

□\square

Remark 6.

In the non-probabilistic setting and for ρ∈(−1,0),\rho\in(-1,0), there exist Wright functions which never vanish on the positive half-line. For ρ∈(−1,−1/2]\rho\in(-1,-1/2] and β>1+ρ,\beta>1+\rho, the function

ϕ⁡(ρ,β,x)=1Γ⁡(γ)​∫−∞xϕ⁡(ρ,1+ρ,−t)​(x−t)γ−1​𝑑t\phi(\rho,\beta,x)\;=\;\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(\gamma)}\int_{-\infty}^{x}\phi(\rho,1+\rho,-t)\,(x-t)^{\gamma-1}\,dt

with γ=1+(1−β)​ρ−1>0,\gamma=1+(1-\beta)\rho^{-1}>0, never vanishes on (0,∞)(0,\infty) since ϕ⁡(ρ,1+ρ,−t)\phi(\rho,1+\rho,-t) is the density of a spectrally negative stable random variable with index −1/ρ-1/\rho, which is positive on ℝ.{\mathbb{R}}. However the function is not integrable at infinity by the asymptotic behaviour

ϕ⁡(ρ,β,x)∼−x(1−β)/ρρ​Γ​(1+(1−β)/ρ)as x→∞,\phi(\rho,\beta,x)\;\sim\;-\frac{x^{(1-\beta)/\rho}}{\rho\,{\Gamma}(1+(1-\beta)/\rho)}\qquad\mbox{as $x\to\infty,$}

with (1−β)/ρ>−1,(1-\beta)/\rho>-1, which is a consequence of Theorem 4 in [41]. Observe also from the same asymptotics that ϕ⁡(ρ,β,x)\phi(\rho,\beta,x) is integrable and takes negative values on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for ρ∈(−1,−1/2]\rho\in(-1,-1/2] and β<1+ρ.\beta<1+\rho. We refer to [29] for an asymptotic study of the zeroes of the Wright function, relying on the original asymptotic behaviours given in [40, 41].

6.3. On the reciprocal convexity of the Mittag-Leffler function

As discussed in the above Remark 3 (i), for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) the reciprocal convexity of the Mittag-Leffler function Eα​(x)E_{\alpha}(x) on the negative half-line is characterized by α≤α∗,\alpha\leq\alpha_{*}, as a by-product of Theorem C. From the asymptotic expansion 18.1.(20) in [11] for α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2) and the works of Wiman [38] for α≥2,\alpha\geq 2, it is known that the function Eα​(x)E_{\alpha}(x) vanishes at least once, and hence cannot be reciprocally convex, on ℝ−{\mathbb{R}}^{-} for all α>1.\alpha>1. We hence have the characterization

1Eαis convex on ℝ−⟺α≤α∗orα=1.\frac{1}{E_{\alpha}}\;\,\mbox{is convex on ${\mathbb{R}}^{-}$}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\alpha\,\leq\alpha_{*}\quad\mbox{or}\quad\alpha=1.

It is interesting to mention that the reciprocal convexity property holds true on the positive half-line for all two-parameter Mittag-Leffler functions Eα,βE_{\alpha,\beta} with α,β≥0.\alpha,\beta\geq 0. Overall, the argument is much simpler than for the if part of Theorem C by the positivity of the coefficients.

Proposition 3.

For every α,β≥0,\alpha,\beta\geq 0, the function

x↦1Eα,β​(x)x\;\mapsto\;\frac{1}{E_{\alpha,\beta}(x)}

is convex on ℝ+.{\mathbb{R}}^{+}.

Proof.

The case α=0\alpha=0 with 1/Eα,β​(x)=Γ⁡(β)​(1−x)+1/E_{\alpha,\beta}(x)={\Gamma}(\beta)(1-x)_{+} is immediate and we will suppose henceforth α>0.\alpha>0. We need to prove that the function

x↦Eα,β​(x)2Eα,β′​(x)x\;\mapsto\;\frac{E_{\alpha,\beta}(x)^{2}}{E_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)}

is non-decreasing on ℝ+.{\mathbb{R}}^{+}. Since the coefficients in the entire series

Eα,β​(x)2=A⁡(x)=∑n≥0an​xnandEα,β′​(x)=B⁡(x)=∑n≥0bn​xnE_{\alpha,\beta}(x)^{2}\;=\;A(x)\>=\;\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}\,x^{n}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad E_{\alpha,\beta}^{\prime}(x)\;=\;B(x)\;=\;\sum_{n\geq 0}b_{n}\,x^{n}

are non-negative, it is enough to show by a classical lemma of [4] that the sequence {un,n≥0}\{u_{n},\;n\geq 0\} is non-decreasing, where

un=anbn=Γ⁡(β+α⁡(n+1))n+1∑k=0n1Γ⁡(β+α​k)​Γ​(β+α⁡(n−k))⋅u_{n}\;=\;\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha(n+1))}{n+1}\,\sum_{k=0}^{n}\,\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha k)\,{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha(n-k))}\cdot

Indeed, this condition entails that the coefficients of the series A′​(x)​B​(x)−A⁡(x)​B′​(x)A^{\prime}(x)B(x)-A(x)B^{\prime}(x) are then all non-negative. For every n≥0,n\geq 0, we compute

un−un−1\displaystyle u_{n}-u_{n-1}\! =\displaystyle= 1n⁡(n+1)​(∑k=0nn​Γ​(β+α⁡(n+1))Γ⁡(β+α​k)​Γ​(β+α⁡(n−k))−∑k=0n−1(n+1)​Γ​(β+α​n)Γ⁡(β+α​k)​Γ​(β+α⁡(n−1−k)))\displaystyle\!\frac{1}{n(n+1)}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{n\,{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha(n+1))}{{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha k)\,{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha(n-k))}\,-\,\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(n+1)\,{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha n)}{{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha k)\,{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha(n-1-k))}\right)

∑k=0nn​vk​vn−k= 2​∑k=1nk​vk​vn−kand∑k=0n−1(n+1)​vk​vn−1−k= 2​∑k=1nk​vk−1​vn−k\sum_{k=0}^{n}\,n\,v_{k}v_{n-k}\;=\;2\;\sum_{k=1}^{n}\,k\,v_{k}v_{n-k}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\,(n+1)\,v_{k}v_{n-1-k}\;=\;2\;\sum_{k=1}^{n}\,k\,v_{k-1}v_{n-k}

Remark 7.

For α≥1\alpha\geq 1 and β≤α,\beta\leq\alpha, it is easy to see that the sequence

(n+1)​Γ​(β+α​n)Γ⁡(β+α+α​n)\frac{(n+1)\,{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha n)}{{\Gamma}(\beta+\alpha+\alpha n)}

is non-increasing and so the function Eα,β​(x)E_{\alpha,\beta}(x) is log-concave on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} by the same argument as above, which implies the reciprocal convexity of Eα,β​(x)E_{\alpha,\beta}(x) on ℝ+.{\mathbb{R}}^{+}. On the other hand, observe that the function Eα,β​(x)=Γ⁡(β)​𝔼​[ex​𝐌α,β−α]E_{\alpha,\beta}(x)={\Gamma}(\beta){\mathbb{E}}[e^{x{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta-\alpha}}] is log-convex on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} for α≤1\alpha\leq 1 and β≥α.\beta\geq\alpha. We refer to [16] for further log-concavity, log-convexity, subadditivity and superadditivity properties of the classical Mittag-Leffler function on the positive half-line.

6.4. A conjecture

The necessary condition given in Theorem D (a) shows that the function ϕ⁡(−α,β,−x)\phi(-\alpha,\beta,-x) is not log-concave on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} for α>α∗​(β).\alpha>\alpha_{*}(\beta). It is easy to show that this can only happen in the subset {0<β<2α−1≤1}\{0<\beta<2\alpha-1\leq 1\} of the admissible set, and that it is equivalent to the condition

Γ⁡(β)​Γ​(β−2​α)Γ​(β−α)2< 1\frac{{\Gamma}(\beta){\Gamma}(\beta-2\alpha)}{{\Gamma}(\beta-\alpha)^{2}}\;<\;1

inside this subset. Moreover, from the asymptotics 18.1.(20) in [11] we have

limz→−∞z6​(2​Eα,α+β′​(z)2−Eα,α+β​(z)​Eα,α+β′′​(z))= 2​(1Γ​(β−α)2−1Γ⁡(β)​Γ​(β−2​α))\lim_{z\to-\infty}\,z^{6}\left(2\,E_{\alpha,\alpha+\beta}^{\prime}(z)^{2}\,-\,E_{\alpha,\alpha+\beta}(z)E_{\alpha,\alpha+\beta}^{\prime\prime}(z)\right)\;=\;2\left(\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(\beta-\alpha)^{2}}\,-\,\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(\beta){\Gamma}(\beta-2\alpha)}\right)

and this shows that the condition α≤α∗​(β)\alpha\leq\alpha_{*}(\beta) is also necessary for the reciprocal convexity of Eα,βE_{\alpha,\beta} on ℝ−.{\mathbb{R}}^{-}. Setting α∗​(0)=α∗​(β)=1\alpha_{*}(0)=\alpha_{*}(\beta)=1 for all β≥1,\beta\geq 1, in view of (13) it is very natural to formulate the following.

Conjecture​​ .

For all admissible (α,β),(\alpha,\beta), one has

α≤α∗​(β)⟺𝐌α,β​has a log-concave density⟺1Eα,α+β​(−t)​is convex on ℝ+.\alpha\,\leq\,\alpha_{*}(\beta)\;\Longleftrightarrow\;{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta}\;\,\mbox{has a log-concave density}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\frac{1}{E_{\alpha,\alpha+\beta}(-t)}\;\,\mbox{is convex on ${\mathbb{R}}^{+}.$}

From the beginning of the proof of Theorem C, we also see that the third property amounts to the concavity on [0,1][0,1] of the function

gα,β​(x)=−x​logα,β⁡(x)+x−1Γ⁡(β)​Γ​(α+β)g_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\;=\;-x\log_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\;+\;\frac{x-1}{{\Gamma}(\beta){\Gamma}(\alpha+\beta)}

where logα,β⁡(x)=Eα,α+β−1​(x)/Γ⁡(α+β)\log_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=E_{\alpha,\alpha+\beta}^{-1}(x)/{\Gamma}(\alpha+\beta) is a generalized logarithm, in other words to the property that the functional in (6) defined with gα,βg_{\alpha,\beta} instead of gαg_{\alpha} is a generalized entropy. Theorems B, C and D show the veracity of this conjecture in the cases β≥α,β=1−α\beta\geq\alpha,\beta=1-\alpha and {α≤4/5,β=0}.\{\alpha\leq 4/5,\beta=0\}. To handle the remaining cases 0<β<α0<\beta<\alpha and {α>4/5,β=0}\{\alpha>4/5,\beta=0\} however, it seems to the authors that other arguments are needed. In particular, in the case β>1−α\beta>1-\alpha we believe, in spite of Remark 6, that 𝐌α,β{\bf M}_{\alpha,\beta} is the positive part of some real self-decomposable spectrally negative random variable, which should obey both the Yamazato property and the bell-shape. We leave this question open for future research.
